items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: I went on to Dallas -- I went to talked to Buster. I said, 'Buster, how would you like to join Nat Toles and go and write some arrangements for him?'

ctx.x:
He was a hell of a first trumpet player, Gary. He started the nanny. You know, like Basie did? I think that's Joe.

So I say, "I think I can get these two Texans." So I says, "You might have to have some money, bring them some money." He said, "Well, that's no --" he said, "Any amount they want." He said, "I can bring that." I said, "Well, you can get them. If you got some money, I know you can get them." So I just told them, I says, "Look, --" Buster said, "I don't want to go back to Bennie Moten." Lester had…

So he says, "Well, could I get some money?" I said, "Yeah, how much you want?" He said, "I don't need but $50.00." I said, "Shit, I'll get you a hundred." So when I went and told Joe, Joe said, "Give me 25. That's all I need." Joe....

items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: I knew him when he was taking lessons from Buster Smith... he always dug Prof

ctx.x: 1934. See, I was with -- I knew him when he was taking lessons from Buster Smith. That's why I know that's authentic, you know, like he always dug Prof and see, Prof used to play like that, although Bird went farther. But that was basically Buster Smith's style. He played like that, alto and soft and runs like Bird. Bird went further, as I say. But that was his idol, was Buster Smith, and he was trying to learn how to play then in '33 and '34.
Was there anything special about him then?

items.title: 56711_Buster Smith oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I think it was Buddy Tate who said that one time he used to play with a plastic reed. [INTERVIEWEE] Yeah. I imagine he did.

ctx.x: Yeah. And he had a stiff reed, kept it on his tenor all the time.
I think it was Buddy Tate who said that one time he used to play with a plastic reed.
